title: Unusual Toxicity With a Protein Degrader Molecule
body_text: Those of you who lived through the worst of the “Rule of Five” era in medicinal chemistry will well appreciate that we are working with a lot of compounds now that cheerfully violate some of those strictures. Molecular weight might be the first on the list, thanks to the number of large bifunctional molecules (for targeted protein degradation and other ideas) that have been in development. In retrospect, there were people (and departments, and whole companies) that put blinders on themselves in an effort to improve their clinical success rates. You can’t blame them for trying - the overall figure is still likely to be 85% per cent failure in the clinic, and you have to pay serious attention to anything that might make that less horrendous. I like to say that that’s the single most important number in the entire biopharma industry, and that pretty much everything that seems weird, puzzling, or outright infuriating about it to outside observers can be traced back to it. But that doesn’t mean that there aren’t problems when you venture into the wilds of chemical space. The Rule of Five was formulated based on the database of approved drugs, and some of that “approval space” really does overlap with better chances of development (as opposed to being just historical accidents of targets, target classes, follow-on structures and so on). High-molecular weight species on average can have more trouble getting through membranes, starting with absorption out of the gut and going on to getting inside cells. And this new toxicology paper is a warning about the other effects that might be waiting out there. The authors (from AbbVie) were developing a bifunctional protein degrader molecule that is only identified in the paper as “Compound X”. We know that it was aimed at a kinase target, but no structure is disclosed. The compound was well into development as a clinical candidate when it ran into dog tox issues. 30 mg/kg daily for five days showed very noticeable liver trouble, and not just of the elevated-blood-enzyme-level variety. Liver enzymes were in fact normal. But the team found degeneration and outright necrosis in the bile ducts, which is not something that I’ve ever come across (and indeed they describe it as “highly unusual”). Histopathology showed trouble in the cholangiocytes cells (vacuoles and debris). Lower doses of the compound were not quite as destructive, but still showed marked abnormalitis in the bile ducts (hyperplasia and signs of inflammation), particularly the large ducts as opposed to the small ones. That profile in particular has apparently never been noted in the toxicology literature, and these changes appeared to be irreversible, unfortunately. Well, that ended things for that compound, obviously. There’s no way you can move forward after a finding like that, but the big question was the mechanistic basis behind this toxicity and how to keep from running into this again. As you will have already guessed, no such effects had been seen in rodents (which is how things got to dog tox anyway, of course). Primary human cholangiocytes were obtained (I’ll bet those back-order pretty quickly) and the compound showed marked cytotoxicity against them, but far lower toxic effects against hepatocytes per se (which lines up with those liver enzyme findings). It seems clear that this compound could have severely injured human subjects or killed them outright. The degrader compound was indeed found in high concentrations by LC/MS in the bile, the bile ducts, and inside the cholangiocytes lining those ducts. You might wonder if degrading the kinase target was the culprit, but that hypothesis didn’t pan out, and neither did assigned blame to the cereblon-targeting end of the degrader molecule. Proteomic studies on those bile duct cells didn’t seem to point to any off-target degradation pathways, but instead showed increases in several proteins, among them several intracellular protein transport pathway members. Closer study showed that there seemed to be some sort of disruption of authophagy and lysosomal function. Comparisons with similar compounds confirmed that protein degradation didn’t seem to be involved in the tox mechanism, and also pointed to physiochemical properties as the culprit, especially overall lipophilicity and the basicity of the linking group of the bifunctional structures. Experienced tox folks might well have expected phospholipidosis as a problem with compounds with a lipophilic/strongly basic profile, but Compound X didn’t really show that in the dogs (while it did show up at higher doses in the mice, but without the bile duct toxicity!) The far-more-easily-obtained U2OS cell line was found to be similarly sensitive to the compounds, and detailed CRISPR experiments in these for sensitivity to over- or under-expression of particular genes zeroed in on increased vacuolar ATPase (V-ATPase) as a very likely culprit. This enzyme is what acidifies late endosomes and lysosomes, making the lysosomal compartment the protein-degrading graveyard that it is. This hypothesis was proven directly by administering Compound X to susceptible cells in the presence of bafilomycin (a known V-ATPase inhibitor natural product), which completely rescued the compound-induced cytotoxicity. Good work! It’s a story that no one would have been able to predict from any first principles, for sure. Mysteries remain. Why was the toxicity so much worse in the large bile ducts than the small ones? There are known differences between the cholangiocytes in these tissues, but we don’t know which of these are important here. Why do these cells take up so much of the compound from the bile, anyway? Why is there such a big difference between the rodent tox and the dog tox? The good news here is that this problem is not peculiar to bifunctional degraders themselves, and seems to have some clear SAR and biophysical signs associated with it. The bad news, though, is that it’s out there waiting for the next compound that has enough bile accumulation and the right properties for the cholangiocytes to want to take it up. It’s something to look out for - and it won’t be the last.
